title: Why Real Communication Is Never Just One Skill
brief: Open by establishing the core problem this unit addresses: in real life, skills do not occur in isolation. Draw directly on the source's rhetorical questions — 'how often do you talk without listening? Or write without reading?' — and its definition of communicative competence as 'the ability to communicate in a target language for meaningful purposes' requiring skills used together in social interaction. Explain the source's distinction between the four primary skills (receptive: listening and reading; productive: speaking and writing) and sub-skills such as grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, and spelling, plus non-verbal skills such as gestures and facial expressions. Close by noting the source's claim that using skills together can lead to better language retention and a more active, motivating classroom — but do not frame these as research findings; present them as the source's stated rationale for integration.

title: A Closer Look at the Integrated Lesson: The Free-Write Activity
brief: Walk through the source's Video Segment 1 classroom activity in detail as the unit's primary worked example of integration in action. Describe how students chose a picture from a magazine, pasted it on paper, wrote about it (either a description or a creative story), and then read it aloud — activating writing, speaking, and listening in sequence. Use the answer key's specifics: one student wrote a factual paragraph about bears; the other wrote fiction about pirates. Explain the 'active listening' technique whereby the non-reading student completed a worksheet during the reading. Note the teacher's role: giving directions, offering praise, and personalising the activity at the end by connecting it to a student's prior interest in bears. Emphasise how the activity demonstrates that one skill (writing) can serve as the spine while reading aloud and listening grow naturally from it.

title: Theme-Based Sequencing: How One Activity Feeds the Next
brief: Explain the principle of theme-based sequencing using the source's own language and examples. Draw on the source's definition of content-based instruction as structuring curriculum or lessons around central themes or topics, and show how this principle is visible in both classroom examples. Use the 'Good Deeds' iEARN project to trace a concrete sequence: students read library materials in jigsaw groups (reading feeds discussion), wrote summaries with citations (reading feeds writing), combined summaries and discussed them as a group (writing feeds speaking and listening), then developed a web page and emailed partner classes (writing feeds authentic communication). Show how each stage produces an output that becomes the input for the next, so the theme holds the sequence together. Do not introduce sequencing frameworks from outside the source.

title: Keeping One Skill as the Lesson's Spine
brief: Address the practical question of how a teacher manages integration without losing focus. Use the source's framing that 'although there is a time to focus attention on just one skill at a time, especially at beginning levels, the final goal is to use skills together for communication.' Apply this to the free-write worked example: writing is the central, assessed skill, but speaking (reading aloud) and listening (the worksheet task) support it without displacing it. Contrast this with the iEARN 'Teddy Bears' project, where oral planning and reading of partner responses supported the spine skill of writing the travel journal. Use the source's activity-skills-resources table structure to show how a teacher can map which skill is primary and which are supporting at each stage of a lesson, keeping the lesson's purpose clear.

title: Adapting Integrated Activities for Different Classroom Contexts
brief: Draw on the source's practical adaptation guidance to show how integrated activities can be scaled and modified. Use the source's suggestions for the free-write activity in larger classes: placing magazines in multiple locations, having students practise reading in pairs before performing for a group, and using the 'chain story' technique where groups of three or four co-author a story in parts — beginning, middle, and end — passing it around in a circle. Note the source's point that stories can be displayed on walls so others can read them. Also draw on the source's note that class-to-class exchange projects have worked successfully via mail without computers, and that teachers without internet access can still set up equivalent projects through local organisations. Frame these as options the source explicitly offers, not as prescriptions.

title: Planning Your Own Integrated Lesson Segment
brief: Guide the learner through the source's four-step action plan for designing an integrated lesson segment. Step 1: reflect on your own classes and consider how integration could improve language retention, motivation, practice opportunities, authentic communication, and classroom activity — all terms drawn directly from the source's action plan. Step 2: design a 15-minute lesson segment that incorporates integrated skills. Step 3: share the plan with peers, explaining what activities come before and after the segment and gathering feedback. Step 4: revise the design, try it, and share results. Encourage the learner to use the activity-tasks-language skills-resources table format modelled in the source as a planning tool. Close by returning to the unit's central idea: that keeping one skill as the spine, while letting others support it around a shared theme, is what makes integration purposeful rather than accidental.
